one_liner: Rust minimal perfect hash (PHast/PHast+) giving ~10 ns queries at under 2 bits/key; about 5x faster queries than PTHash.
what_it_does: The `ph` crate builds a static minimal perfect hash function: for a fixed set of n distinct hashable keys it returns a unique index in 0..n, which you normally use to index your own value array (a static hash table that stores no keys). You build `phast::Function` or `phast::Function2` from a Vec or slice (`from_slice_st`, `from_vec_mt`, or the `with_*_conf_*` constructors that take a seed size, bucket size and a seed chooser such as `SeedOnly` for PHast or `ShiftOnlyWrapped` for PHast+), then call `get(&key) -> usize`. The author recommends `Function2` for PHast+. The same crate also ships the older FMPH/FMPHGO fingerprinting MPHFs, and the git version adds k-perfect (`KFunction`), non-minimal (`Perfect`) and map-or-bump (`Partial`) variants.
how_it_is_fast: PHast is a simplified bucket-placement scheme (the CHD/PTHash family). A 64-bit key hash picks a bucket through a plain linear map, and each bucket stores one fixed-width seed, usually one byte. The value is a linear offset floor(alpha*h) plus p(seed, h) inside a small slice of L values (e.g. 1024), so a query is one hash, one byte load, a multiply and a mask, with no nonlinear bucket function, variable-length seed decoding or rank. Buckets with no feasible seed are 'bumped' (seed 0, about 1% of keys) to further levels whose outputs are remapped through an Elias-Fano array. Construction sorts hashes, seeds buckets from a 256-bucket sliding window with a cyclic used/free bitmap, picks the seed that minimizes the values it occupies, and runs in parallel over chunks separated by small gaps. PHast+ switches to additive placement p = (c + s) mod L, so 64 candidate seeds are tested at once by OR-ing bitmap words; this makes construction about an order of magnitude faster.
when_to_use: Static key sets from millions to hundreds of millions of keys where query latency dominates: at 50M random 10-50-byte string keys PHast answers in 9-12 ns vs 40-54 ns for PTHash and 33-66 ns for PHOBIC.
You need about 1.9-2.1 bits/key and fast (re)builds: PHast+ builds at 61-140 ns/key on one thread and 15-26 ns/key on 12 threads at 50M keys.
Multi-core construction of the smallest fast variant: regular PHast (S=8, lambda=4.3) goes from 606 to 69 ns/key on 12 threads, and parallel construction adds no query-time partitioning step.

Rust code that replaces a read-only HashMap with MPHF + value array (e.g. k-mer or ID indexes). In an informal third-party test (issue #12, u64 keys) PHast + array lookups took 12/20/36 ns at 1M/10M/100M keys, vs 54/80/87 ns for std HashMap and 19/28/30 ns for a GxHash HashMap.
when_not_to_use: The key set changes, or you must reject foreign keys: there is no insert/delete, and `get` has no membership check. A key outside the build set returns an arbitrary index or can panic (open issue #18, no `try_get` yet). Store keys or fingerprints yourself.
C++ projects without a Rust toolchain: the API is Rust-only with no C/C++ bindings. The MPHF-Experiments harness had to write its own `extern "C"` shim to call it.

Key sets that do not fit in RAM: construction takes a Vec or slice and allocates a 64-bit hash per key. Iterator-based construction is only planned (issue #19), and the external-memory algorithm in the paper is not implemented.
Space below about 1.8 bits/key: recursive-splitting methods go lower. PHast needs S=12 and 5,322 ns/key single-thread construction to reach 1.82 bits/key.
Hard worst-case query bounds: bumped keys (about 1%) walk extra levels plus an Elias-Fano lookup, and the default configuration has no constant-level guarantee.

integration.dependencies: bitm, binout, dyn_size_of, seedable_hash (all from the same repo), rayon, voracious_radix_sort, arrayvec; default features add sux, epserde and mem_dbg (aligned-vec on 32-bit targets); optional hash backends: gxhash, wyhash, rapidhash, xxhash-rust, fnv, sip13 (nightly)
integration.min_toolchain: Rust edition 2021. `ph` declares no rust-version, but the default `sux` feature pulls sux/epserde releases that require Rust 1.85; `sip13` needs nightly
integration.platforms: Optimized for 64-bit CPUs; CI builds only on x86-64 Linux with target-cpu=native. The README says it also compiles on 32-bit targets such as wasm32, but slower. The recommended gxhash backend needs x86 AES-NI+SSE2 or ARM AES+NEON and has no fallback
integration.thread_safety: A built function is immutable, and `get(&self)` is read-only; docs.rs lists Send/Sync auto-impls when the hasher and components are Send/Sync, so concurrent queries are fine. Construction is parallel internally (rayon) through the `*_mt` / `threads_num` constructors. No other concurrency guarantees are documented.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it fills the same role as PTHash (static MPHF, get(key) -> [0,n)), but it is a Rust API rather than C++ templates, uses a different serialization format, and has no C++ bindings

gotchas: The default hasher is slow unless you pick one. `ph` depends on seedable_hash with default-features off, so without a hash feature `BuildDefaultSeededHasher` is std's SipHash `DefaultHasher`. A user reported PHast as 'strangely slow' in issue #12 because of this. The paper's numbers use the `gxhash` feature, which needs RUSTFLAGS such as `-C target-cpu=native`.

`write`/`read` serialization requires the same hasher at load time. std's DefaultHasher algorithm is explicitly unspecified across Rust releases, and gxhash output is stable only within a major version, so pin the hasher before persisting functions.
Keys must be distinct (every constructor says so), and construction runs no dedup check. The author warned in issue #2 that duplicate keys make ph (FMPH) construction never finish, so dedupe first.

The API is still 0.x and the released crate lags git. crates.io 0.11.0 (Feb 2026) uses `Params` and `with_slice_p_threads_hash_sc`, while git HEAD uses `Conf` and `with_slice_conf_threads_sc`. PHast docs have no examples. Issue #20 reported that 0.11.0's dependency tree would break on a future rustc.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick PHast over PTHash or PHOBIC when query time matters: at 50M keys it answers in ~10 ns vs 33-66 ns at equal or smaller size (1.94 vs 2.11 bits/key for PTHash with EF). Against PtrHash (the closest rival, also Rust), PHast+ at 50M keys is smaller and at least as fast (2.07 bits/key, 12 ns query, 80 ns/key build vs PtrHash 2.12 bits/key, 14 ns, 192 ns/key cubic), but at 500M keys PtrHash matches its queries; choose SIMDRecSplit, ShockHash or ConsensusRecSplit only when space under ~1.8 bits/key matters more than 100+ ns queries.
verified_claims_summary: The authors' ALENEX26 paper ran the MPHF-Experiments harness on 50M random 10-50-byte string keys (AMD Ryzen 5600G, 6C/12T; rustc 1.84.1 and gcc 12.2.0 at third-level optimization with native CPU flags; GxHash for the Rust methods). PHast (S=8, lambda=4.3, Elias-Fano) used 1.94 bits/key with 10 ns queries vs PTHash (lambda=5, EF) at 2.11 bits/key and 54 ns. Its single-thread build was about 5% slower (606 vs 577 ns/key) but 3.3x faster on 12 threads (69 vs 231 ns/key). At 500M keys the query gap vs PTHash grows (25 vs 135 ns), and PHast+ builds in 61-140 ns/key at 50M keys; there is no comparison against std or CMPH.
status_note: Very active: the author commits almost daily as of 2026-09-25, and PHast research (k-perfect, a new paper) is ongoing. It is MIT OR Apache-2.0 and on crates.io (ph 0.11.0, ~878k downloads), but the released crate trails git and the API is still changing.
